analysis.one_liner: Raises Social Security benefits for low earners, long-time beneficiaries, and students, paid for by higher payroll taxes on high earners.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on December 11, 2019, and died there without a hearing, a vote, or any further action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have raised Social Security benefits in several ways: a minimum benefit tied to the poverty line for people who worked at low wages their whole lives, a benefit bump for people who have been on the program for 16 years or more, and letting children of retired, disabled, or deceased workers keep their benefits through age 26 while in college. To pay for it, the bill would gradually raise the payroll tax rate from 6.2% to 6.5% and apply payroll taxes to earnings above the current cap of about $138,000, which today go untaxed for Social Security. It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Lifetime low earners would get a guaranteed minimum benefit at about the poverty level, with years spent caring for young children counting toward work history. Long-term beneficiaries — disproportionately the oldest retirees and disabled people — would get a benefit increase starting after 16 years on the program. Children of deceased, disabled, or retired workers could keep collecting benefits through age 26 while in college, an age group that currently loses benefits at 19 if not in secondary school. Higher earners above the roughly $138,000 cap and their employers pay the payroll tax increase, but that increase is phased in over six years and applies only to income above the cap (at a declining percentage), so middle-income workers see only the modest across-the-board rate rise.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-earning and long-term Social Security beneficiaries

how_it_helps.text: It creates a new minimum benefit pegged to the poverty line for lifetime low earners, scaled by years worked (counting years spent caring for young children) [S2][S3].
It adds a benefit increase of up to 5% of the benefit for people who have been on Social Security (retirement or disability) for 16 years or more, phasing in at 20% per year [S3].
It lets a child of a retired, disabled, or deceased worker keep receiving benefits through age 26 if they are a full-time college student [S2][S3].
It funds those benefits by gradually raising the payroll tax rate from 6.2% to 6.5% and by phasing in taxation of earnings above the $137,700 cap (90% taxable in 2020, declining thereafter) [S2][S3].

It ensures that the new benefit increases do not count as income for means-tested programs, so beneficiaries do not lose food, housing, or other assistance because their Social Security check rose [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Workers earning above the taxable maximum (about $137,700 in 2020) would pay Social Security tax on earnings above that cap for the first time, at a declining percentage through 2029, and all workers and employers would see the tax rate rise from 6.2% to 6.5% by 2025. Self-employed people would pay the combined increase. Employers' matching share is partly passed to workers in economic analyses, so some cost lands on working people generally.
analysis.who_pays_short: High earners above the tax cap

drawbacks.text: It raises the payroll tax rate from 6.2% to 6.5% on employees and a matching amount on employers over six years [S2][S3]. Workers' take-home pay would fall slightly, and employers bear a matching increase that some would pass along.

The bill applies payroll taxes to earnings above the current cap only at a declining percentage (90% in 2020 down to 0% after 2029) — so even after full phase-in, it does not actually tax earnings above the cap unless the base is later adjusted, which weakens the long-term solvency fix the bill is billed as providing [S3].
Higher payroll taxes on employers are, in standard economic analysis, partly passed back to workers as lower wages over time, which blunts the benefit for some earners.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are broad and the costs fall mostly on the highest earners and their employers, which is the honest trade the bill asks. The drawback an honest supporter would acknowledge is that the payroll tax increase is regressive in form — it applies to wages up to the cap, so middle-income workers pay a bit more (0.3 points eventually, split with employers) — and payroll taxes feed directly into what workers see on paychecks. Set against that, the bill gives new protections (a minimum benefit at poverty level, an old-age benefit bump, longer child benefits) whose value to ordinary households far exceeds that modest increase, and it phases both in slowly. The design is straightforward rather than badly flawed, and it is solvent on its own terms because the benefit increases are paid for by the tax changes.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Gwen Moore introduced the bill on December 11, 2019, and it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the same day [S1][S5].
The full action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action after the referral [S5].
The bill attracted only 4 cosponsors, all Democrats, out of 231 House Democrats [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-income households above the payroll-tax cap and employers, who avoid the higher taxes; the Ways and Means Committee's inaction preserved the status quo where earnings above the cap go untaxed for Social Security.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners above the payroll-tax cap

industries.industry: High-income households (earners above the ~$138,000 payroll-tax cap)
industries.note: They would pay the higher tax rate on wages above the cap as the phase-in proceeds, a cost that falls almost entirely on the top few percent of earners.

Employers would pay a higher matching payroll tax (eventually 6.5% instead of 6.2%) [S3]. Economists expect part of that to be passed back to workers as slower wage growth, so the cost is shared between businesses and employees.
Extending child benefits to age 26 for full-time post-secondary students gives families more ability to keep students enrolled, a modest demand boost for higher education [S3].
